extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, natural history, taxonomy, and philosophy of science (readers learning principles of scientific classification and nomenclature)
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and standards for forming scientific (natural) classifications and nomenclatures: how to choose characters, form groups, handle exceptions, and arrange groups into series to aid induction. Also covers criteria for names and special arrangements when studying particular phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider all varieties before assigning group
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘can not determine the group in which any one object can most conveniently be placed, without taking into consideration all the varieties of existing objects, all at least which have any degree of affinity with it.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assign an object to a class in isolation; classification requires surveying related varieties and affinities across the whole domain to determine the most appropriate grouping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid basing classification solely on simple/perceptible properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial selections for classification are likely to be properties which are simple, easily conceived, and perceptible on a first view (e.g., Tournefort’s corolla shape, Linnaean stamens/pistils), but such selections are often ill-suited to scientific classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of privileging obvious superficial characters merely because they are easy to observe; such bases may group together objects that share little of scientific interest and may be 'mischievous' for habits of thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximize number and importance of common properties in groups
rubrics_metrics.description: The ends of scientific classification are best answered when objects are formed into groups respecting which a greater number of general propositions can be made, and those propositions more important, than could be made of any other grouping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer classifications that permit many and significant generalizations about group members; evaluate candidate groupings by how many and how important the shared properties are.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer causal properties or sure marks as classification bases
rubrics_metrics.description: The properties according to which objects are classified should, if possible, be those which are causes of many other properties; or, at any rate, which are sure marks of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select characters that are causally linked to other traits or reliably indicate them. If the true cause is not directly usable diagnostically, select prominent effects that serve as marks of the cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for natural classification (corresponding to overall likeness)
rubrics_metrics.description: A classification is more scientific when it corresponds to the spontaneous tendencies of the mind by placing together the objects most similar in their general aspect — a 'Natural' classification as opposed to a Technical/Artificial one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor groupings that reflect broad, important resemblances across many properties rather than arbitrary, narrow agreement on one feature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid artificial/technical classifications that impede broader grouping
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical systems arranging things according to their agreement in some arbitrarily selected circumstance often throw together objects with no general resemblance and separate closely similar ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject systems that prioritize convenience of recollection or a single convenient character if they prevent thinking in groups that share many important properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use readily recognizable external marks as proxies for internal characters
rubrics_metrics.description: When the natural basis of classification is internal structure (e.g., anatomy), it is essential that there be some other property or set of properties more readily recognizable by the observer, which co-exist with, and may be received as marks of, the internal properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer external, non-destructive characters that reliably indicate the internal structure; De Blainville’s choice of integument differences is an example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground classification on extensive knowledge of properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Extensive knowledge of the properties of objects is necessary for making a good classification; classification and knowledge tend mutually and indefinitely to improve each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure empirical familiarity with many properties before fixing classificatory schemes; expect iterative improvement as new properties are discovered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Align classification with the intended purpose or use
rubrics_metrics.description: Each science or art forms its classification of things according to the properties which fall within its special cognizance or which it must take account of to accomplish its practical end (e.g., farmer: useful plants vs weeds; geologist: fossils by strata).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the basis of classification appropriate to practical or scientific aims; the same objects may be classified differently for different ends, and such variety is legitimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: For general natural knowledge, prefer attributes that give class individuality
rubrics_metrics.description: When studying objects to extend knowledge of all their properties, consider as most important those attributes which contribute most to render the things like one another and unlike other things — which give to the class the most marked individuality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For broad scientific classification, prioritize attributes that define a class’s distinctive character across many properties rather than narrow or incidental traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine groups by characters (definitions), not solely by type
rubrics_metrics.description: Classes are determined by characters, but these are not arbitrary; the problem is to find a few definite characters which point to the multitude of indefinite ones. Groups should not be decided only by resemblance to a single 'type'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While types (exemplars) are useful for illustration and practical judgment, ensure that explicit characters (diagnostic traits) underlie inclusion in a group so that general propositions are possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure groups have definable characters enabling general assertions
rubrics_metrics.description: If a class did not possess any characters in common, nothing whatever could be predicated of the class; the enumeration of characters is the definition of the species and necessary for making general assertions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define groups by sets of characters (universal or nearly-universal) so that scientific statements about the group can be formulated and tested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include near-exceptional members when overall resemblance is greater
rubrics_metrics.description: A class may include species which lack some of the universal characters; objects that 'straggle' from the central type but resemble the class more than any other should still be included for the ends of scientific classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow for anomalies and exceptions in diagnostic characters if overall affinity and likelihood of sharing yet-undiscovered properties justify inclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select diagnostic characters that indicate shared parentage and predict further properties
rubrics_metrics.description: The problem is to find a few definite characters which point to the multitude of indefinite ones; the characters should be those by which we might recognize the possibility of a common parentage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose characters that are reliable indicators of deeper relations (e.g., heredity or developmental commonality) and that help predict other properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid basing classification on solitary arbitrary characters lacking broader relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Classes formed on properties like the exact number of stamens and pistils may lead to groups for which little of use can be predicated; such properties are of little importance and remembering them with accuracy is of no moment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject bases that yield groups with few meaningful shared properties merely for mnemonic convenience; prefer characters with explanatory or predictive value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and adopt distinctions of Kind wherever they exist
rubrics_metrics.description: Every natural classification shall recognize and adopt into itself all distinctions of Kind which exist among the objects it classifies; to pass over any distinctions of Kind would be to replace classes with more attributes by classes with fewer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where genuine, deep distinctions of Kind are present, classification must reflect them; Kinds imply pervasive differences across many properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form series when investigating particular phenomena (arrange by degree)
rubrics_metrics.description: For investigating the laws of a phenomenon, erect into one class all Kinds where that phenomenon presents itself and arrange those kinds in a series according to the degree in which they exhibit it — beginning with those which exhibit most and ending with those which exhibit least.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the classificatory objective is the study of a specific phenomenon, arrange taxa in graduated series to enable the Method of Concomitant Variations and to identify causal or correlative relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bring together all Kinds exhibiting the phenomenon for inductive study
rubrics_metrics.description: The requisites of a classification for facilitating the study of a particular phenomenon are first to bring into one class all Kinds of things which exhibit that phenomenon, in whatever variety of forms or degrees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that the dataset for inductive inference includes all relevant Kinds exhibiting the phenomenon to avoid biased or incomplete induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish a type-species/genus for special inductive inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the classification is made for the express purpose of a special inductive inquiry, it is necessary to establish a type-species or genus which exhibits in the most eminent degree the particular phenomenon under investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select exemplar taxa that most clearly illustrate the phenomenon as anchors for arranging series and for focusing inductive analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct nomenclature to convey maximum significant information
rubrics_metrics.description: A nomenclature is a system of the names of Kinds; the only merit beyond definition is to convey, by the mode of their construction, as much information as possible about the Kind (either by indicating properties or nearest affinities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer names that (where practicable) indicate diagnostic properties; otherwise, use names that embed the proximate natural group (binary nomenclature) to convey useful connotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use hierarchical (binary/ternary) names to economize and manage many species
rubrics_metrics.description: By incorporating the name of the genus (and, if needed, the family/order) into the species name (binary or ternary nomenclature), one economizes on the number of distinct names necessary and conveys proximal affinities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt hierarchical naming (e.g., Linnaean binomial) to reduce memory burden and to pack informative affinity into names; ternary names may be used where binary is insufficient.
